title: with the Keeper's framing of what the tradition has kept and rejected
word: with the Keeper's framing of what
hook: when a rule and your heart disagree: a law book that names the heart among the roots of dharma
carry: with the Keeper's framing of what the tradition has kept and rejected
tomorrow: so is weighing it all just picking and choosing?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ambedkar's fire: a book refused in public, and a constitution that abolished untouchability. Now, one question.

When a rule and your gut disagree, which one do you trust? Group chats argue about it all the time. The Manusmriti, of all books, has something to say. Before its second chapter hands down a single rule, it says dharma is what good people, free of hatred and grasping, approve in their hearts. And a few verses later, it goes further.
screen: `THE RULE, OR YOUR GUT?` → `APPROVED IN THEIR HEARTS.` → `A FEW VERSES LATER…`

segments.voice: It names the roots of dharma. In paraphrase: the Veda, the smriti, the conduct of good people, and what is pleasing to one's own self. Four roots, and the last is the surprise. Commentators call it atmatushti, the self's contentment, and it sits in a law book's own list. Readers take it in different ways. Some read it narrowly: it counts only where the first three leave a choice open. Others hear in it a place for conscience inside the tradition. A neighbor tradition says something close. In his letter to the Romans, Paul writes of people who don't have the law yet do what it asks, and who, in the King James words, "shew the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience also bearing witness." Shared: two old texts that say right and wrong are written somewhere inside a person, not only on a page. And an honest difference. Paul is speaking of people outside the law, whose conscience bears witness anyway. Manu puts the heart inside a law book, last of four roots, after the Veda, the remembered books and the conduct of the good. One asks how people without the law can know right; the other, what the law itself leans on. Neither is ranked here. Both leave room for the heart.
screen: `FOUR ROOTS OF DHARMA.` · `THE LAST: ATMATUSHTI.` · `ROMANS: WRITTEN IN THEIR HEARTS.` · then, large: `BOTH LEAVE ROOM FOR THE HEART.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes, and bring to mind one choice in front of you right now. Without deciding anything, notice what sits easy in your heart and what doesn't, the way you'd notice warm air and cool. If you pray, you can hold the choice before God.
Kept and rejected, weighed by a root inside the law: atmatushti, the self's contentment, last of Manu's four roots of dharma.
Your line: what the tradition has kept and rejected is weighed, at last, by what sits right in a good heart. More tomorrow.

Unity thread (wisdom day, and this month's meeting with the best friend's family): shared with Christianity, in its own words (Romans 2:15, KJV): right and wrong written within a person. Honest difference: Paul speaks of Gentiles without the law whose conscience bears witness (2:14); Manu places the self's contentment inside a law book, last of four roots. Neither ranked; not 'all the same'. 1574 used Judaism (Leviticus 19), so this week's neighbor differs. Sam's grandmother (Christian family, per earlier notes) quotes the line in the chat.

KJV Romans 2:15 reads 'Which shew the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience also bearing witness, and their thoughts the mean while accusing or else excusing one another;' the quotation uses the middle of the verse exactly. Confirm.
'Four roots' is the text's own count (2.12 calls them fourfold). Manu's wording is 'ātmanas tuṣṭi' (2.6) and 'svasya ca priyam ātmanaḥ' (2.12); 'atmatushti' is the commentators' term. Confirm.
'Some read it narrowly… others hear a place for conscience' summarizes a known range of readings (e.g. commentators who limit it to optional matters); confirm or name.
